title: Warm-gain dominance did not isolate thermal sorting in two Northeast Shelf plankton samples
abstract: We tested whether warm-taxon gains or cold-taxon losses supplied more community warming in NOAA EcoMon samples from 1992-2023. We used matched seasonal coverage in 65 zooplankton cells and 60 fish-larva cells. Thermal scores used early records outside each target spatial block. An exact finite-change budget gave a zooplankton net thermal shift of +0.0557 C. Warm gains supplied +0.0869 C, cold losses +0.0512 C and opposing changes -0.0824 C. The warm-gain minus cold-loss contrast was +0.0357 C, with a planned 97.5% crossed-bootstrap interval of 0.0020 to 0.1076 C. Raw density weights gave an interval that included zero. The main fish contrast also included zero. Added thermal-label shuffles gave one-sided contrast probabilities of 0.077 and 0.976. The zooplankton net shift exceeded its shuffled reference, but gain dominance did not clearly do so. A proportional-growth counterexample proves that gain dominance can occur with no thermal sorting. These results limit a process interpretation of strong marine tracking. They do not identify climate effects or explain the terrestrial gap. One survey, internal thermal labels, sparse blocks, noisy sign splits and imperfect shuffle exchangeability limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, input hashes and reproduction steps are included. Raw data remain external.

display.caption: Exact thermal budgets and gain-loss contrasts for two marine assemblages. Primary budgets use log density. Contrasts are sensitive to weights.
